The Hyundai IONIQ 5 is the most popular EV in America outside of Tesla, but its larger three-row sibling looks like the better deal right now.
Hyundai IONIQ 5 vs IONIQ 9 lease comparison
Through September, the Hyundai IONIQ 5 was the third top-selling EV in the US, behind the Tesla Model Y and Model 3.
Hyundai’s electric SUV is outselling rivals like the Chevy Equinox EV, Ford Mustang Mach-E, and Toyota bZ.
Why? For one, it’s one of the most affordable EVs in the US, starting at about $35,000, and Hyundai has been offering some of the most attractive lease deals.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
After the $7,500 federal EV tax credit expired at the end of September last year, Hyundai responded by reducing prices on the IONIQ 5 by up to nearly $10,000 on some trims.
The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,250. That’s for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. Upgrading to the extended-range SE RWD model adds $2,500, starting at $37,750, and offers up to 318 miles of range.
2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 (Source: Hyundai)
Hyundai’s three-row electric SUV, the IONIQ 9, starts at $58,955, or nearly $24,000 more than the base IONIQ 5 SE.
On Hyundai’s website, the 2027 IONIQ 5 SE Standard Range is available to lease from $359 a month. The offer is for a 24-month lease with $4,999 due at signing for an effective cost of $567 per month.
Hyundai IONIQ 9 at HMGMA test track (Source: Hyundai)
The extended-range Hyundai IONIQ 5 SE RWD can be leased from $369 a month. The offer is also a 24-month lease with $4,999 due at signing, for an effective cost of $577 per month.
Hyundai’s larger IONIQ 9, meanwhile, is available to lease from $419 a month. That deal also includes $4,999 due at signing, but is for a 36-month lease, so the effective cost is $557 per month.
Using Hyundai’s payment calculator , it would cost about $412 a month to lease the 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 SE for 36 months with $4,999 due at signing. With an effective cost of $550 per month, it’s only $7 less than the three-row IONIQ 9.
2026 Hyundai IONIQ 9 interior (Source: Hyundai)
The Hyundai IONIQ 9 offers more range than its smaller sibling, with an EPA-estimated range of up to 335 miles for the base SE trim.
The IONIQ 5 is a midsize electric SUV, about the same size as a Tesla Model Y, with two rows and enough room for five passengers. Hyundai’s larger IONIQ 9 offers three rows of seating and six- or seven-seat configurations.
Hyundai IONIQ 5 interior (Source: Hyundai)
With an added row of seating, the IONIQ 9 offers up to 163.54 cubic feet of interior passenger volume, compared with the IONIQ 5, which offers up to 106.5 cubic feet.
While the IONIQ 9 may be the better deal right now, the IONIQ 5 is still a good fit for those looking for a smaller, more efficient SUV that doesn’t necessarily need the added space.
Which one would you choose? The IONIQ 5 or IONIQ 9? Let us know why in the comments.
Hyundai’s electric vehicle conquest rates (Source: Peter Johnson/ Electrek/ Hyundai)
Both the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 are built at Hyundai’s Metaplant America outside of Savannah, Georgia.
When we toured the facility earlier this year, Hyundai told us that its electric SUVs are attracting new buyers to the brand at a higher rate than its gas or hybrid vehicles.
The IONIQ 5 had a 69.8% conquest rate last year, while the IONIQ 9 had 64.3%. Hyundai’s Elantra N ranked third (61.9%), followed by the Palisade (61.2%) and Kona Electric (60.9%).

iScooter's Latest i10M E-Scooter Promises a Lot for $500 – Built To Handle City Use and Then Some
15 photos
Photo: iScooter
With gas prices showing no signs of coming back down anytime soon, I've decided to explore other and more affordable means of moving around our cities. One of the most called-upon in recent times has been the e-scooter, and today, we explore an option that costs just $500, while boasting some solid abilities.
It’s called the i10M and is the creation of none other than iScooter, a brand that has been in this business since 2018, so clearly, they have some idea of what it takes to produce e-scooters; that’s eight years.
Photo: iScooter As we can see, one way this brand hooks new riders is with the price tag, and if I may, for the $500 that we dish out for this electrified two-wheeler, it’s actually able to handle its own weight against other more expensive units pretty well.
While the price was only a factor in sparking my interest in this EV, as I dove in deeper, I could see gear and systems often used on e-scooters I've tested, so I have some idea of what we can expect from this one.
First and foremost, this is a single-motor option, with the powerhouse stuffed into the rear hub. What I also liked are the covers that iScooter has tossed over the motor, granting a clean look, but also one that protects the system from debris and light splashes. An IPX4 rating is mentioned on the manufacturer’s website.
Keep in mind that one small inconsistency that I stumbled across is the water and dustproofing; another section of the website mentions an IP54 rating, so dust is kept at bay too.
Photo: iScooter This motor can produce a peak of up to 1,200 W, so it’s not the most powerful out there, but iScooter didn’t aim to build the fastest or strongest out there, but rather, a commuter option that still keeps things legal with a top speed of up to 28 mph (45 kph) and doesn’t sap your battery like a stronger system.
It’s not clear just how much torque the motor can produce or what sort of slopes we can tackle in our towns, but we do know that riders of as much as 120 kg (265l bs) are suitable for the i10M as it’s tuned to operate on a 48 V ecosystem.
One aspect where I feel we could have been granted access to a bit more is in the range department. According to iScooter, around 25 miles (40 km) is the peak range that we can see out of the 10.4 Ah battery that is standard on this model. Not so much, especially if we encounter hills and rougher terrain, not to mention having a lunch that’s too big.
Once drained, it can take up to 6 hours for a full recharge.
Photo: iScooter What I did like about the i10M is the suspension. A tried and tested C-arm setup is used here, and if there’s one thing I know about this suspension, it’s that it can also handle off-road use, expanding our two-wheeling playground to beyond the tarmac.
While this is a solid setup, iScooter does claim that this places rocky paths on the menu, along with forest trails, and other less-groomed surfaces. Personally, I'd be careful trying to fly around at full speed on these surfaces, but you get the idea, and to thank is the suspension.
What I'd like to point out is that I don’t see a traditional shock in the works, but rather, something that looks more like a torsion axle, and probably calls upon a rubber of kinds to facilitate the action. The spec sheet mentions “front and rear double shock absorbers” nothing else.
In terms of safety and control, we have the brakes, and while I've never been a fan of cable-actuated brakes, for the top speed this one can catch, they should be fine. But, iScooter also adds another layer of braking in the form of e- ABS , helping slow down the i10m that much more .
Photo: iScooter Tire compound also plays an important role in just how little space we come to a complete stop, so be sure to look around at other options if you test the i10M and are not happy with how past those locked up tires (11-inch tubeless) come to a halt.
Since there is an app and digital display, we may be able to tamper with certain settings, but for the time being, the limited details don't support this notion.
To help you maneuver this one around town in case you encounter a flight of stairs, a folding frame is also worked into the whole thing. Complete it with lighting at the front and rear, and we have ourselves a decent-looking option for $500, don’t you think?
I’m actually curious to hear if you’d be happy with around 25 miles of range for $500 considering that the average American travel around 35 miles or so daily by car; drop a comment below and ride safe out there.

B2Gold President and CEO Mike Cinnamond at hte Mining Forum Americas last month in Colorado.
Posted By: Henry Lazenby October 23, 2026
B2Gold (TSX: BTO; NYSE-A: BTG) aims to turn its troubled Goose mine in Nunavut into a 300,000-oz.-a-year gold producer once crushing upgrades are complete, President and CEO Mike Cinnamond says.
The Vancouver-based miner is expanding an undersized crushing circuit that also suffered fire damage in April. It targets full processing capacity of 4,000 tonnes a day by mid-2027. Cinnamond maintained Goose’s production forecast of 170,000 to 200,000 oz. for this year, with higher throughput and stronger grades expected to support a bigger fourth quarter.
“We’re flipping, we’re turning around, we’re starting to pull cash flow in,” Cinnamond told The Northern Miner late last month in Colorado Springs. “The repairs are a key test of B2Gold’s shift from heavy construction spending to generating more cash for shareholders.”
New ore supplies from Fekola Regional in Mali are expected to add production as they ramp up next year, while gold-price contracts that limit the company’s upside expire in January. Delivering those operational gains would give the miner more room to fund growth and share buybacks, with Cinnamond favouring opportunities within its portfolio as acquisitions elsewhere become more expensive.

Florida Canyon, Nevada. ( Image courtesy of Integra Resources. )
Posted By: Henry Lazenby October 23, 2026
Integra Resources (TSXV: ITR; NYSE-A: ITRG) needs fourth-quarter gold production to rise at least 32% from the previous three months to meet its annual target, even after reporting a second quarterly increase in output at its Florida Canyon mine in Nevada.
The operation, about 72 km southwest of Winnemucca, produced 17,652 oz. in the third quarter, taking nine-month output to 46,666 ounces. Meeting the production guidance that was on Thursday left unchanged at 70,000 to 75,000 oz. requires another 23,334 to 28,334 oz. before year-end, a 32% to 61% quarterly increase.
“Mining rates are expected to remain elevated this quarter as we focus on annual production guidance,” President and CEO George Salamis said Thursday in a release.
Florida Canyon is Integra’s only operating mine and a source of funding for its development pipeline, including the main DeLamar project in Idaho. The production target tests whether spending on equipment, waste removal and leach pads can turn higher mining rates into more saleable gold.
Integra’s Toronto-listed shares traded down 1.9% at $3.12 in afternoon trading Friday, having touched $2.80 and $6.60 over the past year. The company has a market capitalization of $632.7 million (US$451.9 million).
Improving trend
Higher second-half output was already part of the plan. In February, Integra forecast about 45% of annual production in the first six months. In August, management said increased ore placement had built an inventory of recoverable gold expected to support stronger production through year-end.
Third-quarter production rose 8% from the preceding quarter, while ore mined increased 21% to 5.35 million tonnes and ore placed on leach pads climbed 25% to 5.21 million tonnes. The processed grade improved to 0.25 gram gold per tonne from 0.23 gram.
Reported gold recovery fell to 52.5% from 57.8% in the second quarter. Integra attributed the decline to increased placement of uncrushed ore, which has lower expected recovery than crushed material. The company said it is monitoring and refining the blend as mining rates increase.
Thursday’s operations update doesn’t quantify how much fourth-quarter production is expected from gold already on the pads, new ore placement or changes in recovery. It also doesn’t give a fourth-quarter production forecast.
Work to remove waste above the Central Pit remains a priority, with improved access to higher-grade ore expected next year. Investment at Florida Canyon will continue into 2027 at a lower rate, Salamis said.
Cost test
Integra reported a preliminary cash balance of US$119.5 million at Sept. 30, compared with US$111.1 million three months earlier. The increase doesn’t establish how much cash the mine generated after investment; full quarterly financial results are slated for release on Nov. 11.
Integra documents show annual mine-site all-in sustaining cost guidance of US$3,300 to US$3,500 per oz. sold. That forecast, increased earlier this year, provides another test of whether higher output can spread spending over more ounces.
The company is also advancing DeLamar through permitting toward a construction decision in the second half of 2027, while completing economic studies and work ahead of permitting at Nevada North.

Less-than-truckload carrier Roadrunner announced a new outbound Canada-to-U.S. service on Friday. It also announced a 5.9% general rate increase, which will be effective on Nov. 2.
Roadrunner’s ( OTC: RRTS ) new service connects shippers across Canada to approximately 40 major metro markets in the U.S. The direct linehaul service is executed entirely by truck, with no shipments touching the railroads.
“We built a proprietary Smart Network for direct, long-haul, metro-to-metro service, delivering fewer handling points, faster transit, real-time visibility, and greater accountability with no unnecessary transfer points to delay shipments or compromise visibility,” said Dave Black, vice president of strategic sales at Roadrunner. “We have focused primarily on strengthening our U.S. network, and we are pleased to announce our next phase of expansion.”
Roadrunner was already serving U.S.-outbound lanes into Canada . Its metro-to-metro, long-haul network utilizes independent drivers and over 40 terminals to provide LTL service to shippers.
The GRI is expected to average 5.9% across general tariff codes and lanes. The announcement follows other recent rate implementations from carriers.
“To support expansion and further investment in better offerings, we’re introducing the GRI to sustain investment in our leading network,” said Nathalie de Champlain, chief transformational officer. “The adjustment addresses increased costs driven by market conditions and supports continued investment in network efficiency and service quality.”
Why it matters? Roadrunner’s new direct, truck-only Canada-to-U.S. service provides LTL shippers with faster transit, fewer handling points and improved visibility across roughly 40 major U.S. metro markets. Additionally, its 5.9% GRI highlights how carriers are adjusting prices to combat rising operating costs and invest in their networks.

Unmanned systems now inflict more than 90% of Russia’s casualties on the front lines in Ukraine, yet no NATO military, including America’s, has begun the overhaul that kind of war demands, Ret. Army Gen. David Petraeus said Oct. 16, weeks after the Pentagon announced a new command for autonomous warfare.
The extent of the drone war is underestimated, with Ukraine and Russia each using roughly 10,000 drones a day, the former CIA director and onetime commander of U.S. Central Command said, speaking at an American Primary Aluminum Association event in Washington.
“This is an unmanned systems war,” Petraeus said . “Tanks aren’t survivable there anymore.”
For Ukraine, drones and unmanned weapons have become central to how the country has leveraged a smaller, outgunned force against a much larger, better-financed adversary for almost five years.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy ordered the creation of a new Unmanned Systems Forces military branch in 2024, and the Defense Ministry has said time and again that developing more autonomous weapons is a top priority.
But for the rest of the world, Petraeus said, the fighting in Ukraine is a window into the future and a warning about the dangers of being underprepared for the battles to come.
“Really, no NATO country and not even the United States is undertaking yet the urgent revolutionary institutional change that should be taken based on what we see in Ukraine, which is the future of war,” he said.
The U.S. needs a new concept of warfare that runs through force structure, training, procurement, personnel policy and bases, the general said, replacing much of the legacy, heavily manned equipment with unmanned systems that are cheaper and far more numerous.
“What’s going to happen is we’ll see the introduction of autonomous systems really for the first time in warfare,” Petraeus said.
Washington is making “some commendable steps” toward developing these weapons, according to Petraeus, including establishing a new Autonomous Warfare Command that requires each military branch to stand up its own component command.
“But my hope is that they will not just create an unmanned systems force in terms of force structure, but that they will also spur the initiation of true institutional change,” Petraeus said.
That includes how the U.S. buys weapons, Petraeus said, calling for “very, very substantial manufacturing capacity but not necessarily producing all the time.”
“You want it to be able to make software changes every week, hardware changes every few weeks, which is what’s going on in Ukraine because the enemy continues to evolve and Russia’s been innovating very substantially as well,” he said.
Ukraine will produce as many as 20 million unmanned systems this year, Zelenskyy said in a July speech , with a shortage of trained operators and the acquisition of some weapons components — including optics, gimbals, brushless motors and fiber-optic cable — becoming the domestic industry’s production bottleneck.
The general also rejected the idea that the U.S. war with Iran has hurt Washington’s ability to help Kyiv, though he acknowledged the U.S. has used “a fair number of missile interceptors,” which “makes it more difficult to share those with others around the world.”
The war has consumed between one-half and two-thirds of the U.S. inventory of certain missile-defense interceptors, according to a Congressional Budget Office estimate released in September.
“We can help the Ukrainians in any way in which we decide to assist them,” Petraeus said. “These are policy decisions.”

Katie Livingstone is the Ukraine correspondent for Defense News and Military Times. Based in Kyiv, she has covered Russia's full-scale invasion since its first days. She is a former Fulbright fellow whose award-winning work has appeared in outlets across Europe and the U.S.

Aerowave Is a Monorail Concept That Isn't So Far From Being a Reality – Similar Ideas Already Exist
14 photos
Photo: Enise Topbas
There are countless modes of moving around our world, and one of them is the monorail. Oh, and before you disregard this style of transport, keep in mind that there are companies out there banking on this sort of system. Heck, we even have some moving people around the US as we speak.
Today, on the other hand, we’ll be exploring a conceptual system, and not one that actually exists, at least, not yet. It’s called the Aerowave and is a design from the mind of Enise Topbaş, an industrial designer from Turkey, and while not everyone sees monorails as a viable solution for urban transport, there are companies out there that are chasing this dragon, so we could, one day, see an “Aerowave” flying around our cities and outskirts.
Photo: Enise Topbas Now, the very first monorail designs were seen on paper as early as 1821 and over the years, there have been countless spins on the idea before we finally reached the systems we have in place today.
Currently, monorails are typically massive and train-like constructions that weave through cities, often, suspended above the ground. Usually, hundreds of people can be transported at a time with a monorail.
Aerowave, on the other hand, takes the ‘hundreds’ out of the equation and reduces the number down to just one; it’s a single-occupancy solution and one that, if I may, looks absolutely amazing!
Each pod is constructed from a blend of materials including metal for the chassis and lower half, and a whole lot of glass on the upper part. The latter also makes for some very amazing views as we’re being transported around town, and if I may, the design of this pod is all so very futuristic; it fits perfectly in a scene in some Sci-Fi movie or series.
Photo: MonoCab Believe it or not, it also fits into the modern age, if only as an idea. Hear me out.
Back in 2018, a German team won an award for presenting a monorail system (CountryCab, now MonoCab) that is oh so similar to Aerowave, sustaining the idea that such a concept is a solution that some companies are willing to back.
Much like Aerowave, only one single rail was to be used by the MonoCab, and each pod was also suitable only for one person. It was to be used as a taxi service in rural areas where trains once ran but their lines remained.
What was rather neat about the CountryCab was that, indeed, it utilized old and existing tracks, meaning that part of the infrastructure already exists, making for an easy implementation of the system. Since the cabs use only one rail, the railway tracks also allow the system to function each way. One line heads east, and the other west, so to speak, or north and south, or whichever way they run.
Photo: MonoCab Furthermore, CountryCab also called upon gyroscopic abilities to stay upright, but the Aerowave does not; the latter is more like a traditional monorail, that are in use today but calling upon a much narrower track due to the size of the pods themselves.
In order to function on existing tracks like the MonoCab, the Aerowave system will need to be modified in some way. Either the cab sees modifications in order to be accommodated to rail width and height, or the rails themselves will need to see modifications to support the pod.
Enise does showcase the pods on a rail that doesn’t look anything like an existing system, so to implement an Aerowave, we’ll need a completely new infrastructure.
Photo: Enise Topbas Since the concept is one that’s designed to function as a personal cab and taxi service, an app is showcased on the ideation page. You can order a pod directly from your phone, travel to the nearest hub or boarding station, hop in, and enjoy the ride. Costs will simply be drawn from your account via the app, much like any modern payment service.
Now, sure, for the time being, the Aerowave is a concept, and one that we probably won’t see being called upon for another couple of decades, if ever, but it doesn’t hurt to dream a little. After all, all that we see started off as nothing more than an idea on paper or a few scribbles on a napkin. Yet, the costs involved in implementing a fresh layer of transportation will cost millions. Any takers?
Personally, I'd love to be alive in a time where a personal transport system like the Aerowave is available, even with the whole glass bubble look. Aside from being used as a transportation service, with the whole glass look and nighttime city lights on full blast, it would be a downright pleasure to hop into a pod and just have it carry you around the city while you listen to your favorite tunes. One hell of a way to wind down after a long day in Babylon.

source_document.body:
Wabtec reported higher third-quarter revenue and earnings and raised its outlook as the company’s freight and transit equipment backlogs grew.
Operating income increased 27%, to $625 million, as revenue grew 8%, to $3.12 billion, the company said Wednesday. Earnings per share increased 34%, to $2.42. Wabtec (NYSE: WAB ) raised its full-year adjusted EPS guidance to a range of $10.85 to $11.05, an increase of 21% to 23.2%, up from the prior outlook of an increase of 18.2% to 21.5%.
“The strength of our performance reflects our momentum across the portfolio, disciplined execution by our teams, and the continued success of our strategic actions. These actions enhance our growth profile, expand margins, and increase the earnings power of the company,” Chairman and Chief Executive Rafael Santana said in a release. “Our teams continue to translate healthy customer demand into profitable growth while investing in technologies that will advance the future of transportation. These investments are strengthening our competitive position and reinforcing Wabtec as a leading industrial technology company.”
Freight segment revenue increased 6.9% in the quarter, with digital intelligence revenue up 24.2% thanks to Wabtec’s acquisition of Frauscher Sensor Technologies and what it said was strong demand.
Wabtec received new locomotive and modernization orders worth $633 million from two Class I railroads. It did not name the railroads.
Growth in North American freight traffic this year has prompted Class I railroads to reactivate stored locomotives, which has led to increased parts orders, Santana told investors and analysts on the company’s earnings call. But Wabtec has yet to see the volume growth translate into orders for new locomotives, he said.
The Freight segment’s 12-month backlog rose 7.5% from a year earlier, to $6.54 billion.
Transit segment revenue increased 11.3%, to $883 million, driven by the acquisition of Dellner Couplers of Sweden and higher original equipment and aftermarket sales. The Transit segment’s 12-month backlog increased 12.2%, to $2.45 billion.
Why it matters: Wabtec’s third-quarter report shows a recovery in railroad equipment use without yet signaling a broad rebound in new-equipment spending.

source_document.body:
Drewry’s World Container Index rose 2% to $4,585 per 40-foot container, supported by higher rates on trans-Pacific and Asia-Europe routes as strong U.S. import demand and carrier capacity cuts bolstered pricing.
Shanghai-to-Los Angeles rates increased 2% to $8,007 per 40-foot container, while Shanghai-to-New York rates edged up 1% to $10,166. Drewry expects trans-Pacific rates to remain stable next week, with U.S. import demand continuing to support the market despite an increase in available capacity.
Carriers have announced only two blank sailings on the trans-Pacific for next week, down from six this week, according to figures from Drewry’s Container Capacity Insight. The service tracks scheduled and canceled sailings, effective capacity and port congestion across major trade lanes.
Rates from Shanghai to Rotterdam rose 3% to $3,632 per 40-foot container, while Shanghai-to-Genoa rates increased 5% to $4,152.
Unlike the trans-Pacific, the Asia-Europe trade faces more sailing cancellations next week. Carriers have announced eight blank sailings, up from two this week, tightening available capacity as they seek to put upward pressure on freight rates.
Drewry expects Asia-Europe rates to increase slightly next week as capacity reductions support pricing.
The cuts come as congestion at key Asian ports eases. Vessel waiting times at Shanghai fell from 97 hours in Week 38 to 38 hours in Week 42, signaling a substantial improvement in port operations.
Security risks and attacks on ships continue to affect vessel movements through the Persian Gulf. Only two containerships sailed into the Gulf in Week 42, down from five the previous week. Meanwhile, sailings through the Suez Canal increased slightly, from 54 in Week 41 to 55 in Week 42.
Why it matters: The increase signals continued cost pressure on importers, even as congestion at major Asian ports eases. Strong U.S. demand is supporting trans-Pacific rates, while Asia–Europe carriers are canceling more sailings to tighten available space and bolster pricing, leaving shippers’ costs dependent on both cargo demand and carrier capacity decisions.

source_document.body:
Bannerman's Etango uranium project in Namibia. ( Image courtesy of Bannerman Energy. )
Posted By: Colin McClelland October 23, 2026
Bannerman Energy (ASX, NSX: BMN; US-OTC: BNNLF) and its Chinese partner CNNC Overseas have approved construction of the Etango uranium project in Namibia, with funding secured without project debt and first production targeted for 2028.
The development is expected to cost $353 million (about C$494 million) before production and deliver an average of 3.5 million lb. of uranium oxide annually. About $64 million has already been spent on early works, leaving roughly $289 million in pre-production spending, Bannerman said in its announcement Friday. The decision moves Etango into full-scale construction after years of studies and preparatory work.
“[The FID] is the culmination of more than two decades of exploration, study and disciplined de-risking, and it formally commits the JV to full-scale construction of the world-class Etango Uranium Project,” Chamberlain said in a release.
“Etango is set to be a long-life, large-scale producer in Namibia’s Erongo region, a highly established uranium province, at a time when the world’s utilities increasingly need secure, diversified supply.”
The approval follows a September financing deal with CNNC Overseas, part of China National Nuclear Corp., that secured both construction capital and a buyer for most of Etango’s output. Bannerman owns 55% of the joint venture and CNNC Overseas holds 45%. The venture owns 95% of Etango.
Bannerman shares fell 4.2% to A$3 apiece in Sydney on Friday, valuing the company at roughly A$748 million. Ahead of the construction decision, UBS retained its Buy rating but cut its price target 17% to A$4.39 to reflect dilution from recent equity raisings, FNArena reported . The bank considered Etango fully funded.
CNNC main buyer
Under the financing arrangement , the Chinese partner invested $320.4 million, including $294.5 million in the joint venture. It will buy 60% of Etango’s lifetime production on market-based terms without price floors or ceilings. Bannerman retains independent marketing rights over the remaining 40%.
The venture held about $295 million in cash at Sept. 30 to cover remaining pre-production spending. Bannerman separately held about A$175 million, which it said fully funds its remaining share of working capital through construction, ramp-up and targeted commercial production. The capital estimate carries a range of plus or minus 10%.
Etango’s approved design calls for an open pit and heap-leach operation processing 8 million tonnes annually.
Namibia awarded the mining licence in December 2023 , and environmental approvals cover the proposed mine and supporting infrastructure. Bannerman’s September construction update put bulk earthworks at 99% complete. About 86% of concrete for the first two contracted packages had been poured, while the first stage of the permanent water pipeline was about 90% complete.
